subtype_label: Focus internal / focus inference (no given focus)
query: Help me understand what's worth analyzing and actionable in these expense records.

judge.implied_focus: Expense processing quality and spending magnitude — surfacing anomalies/risk in expense records (large amounts, processing delays, missing metadata, high-volume submitters)

per_column.name: amount_tier
per_column.rationale: Buckets expense magnitude into Low/Medium/High, a directly actionable facet for flagging high-value spend worth scrutiny.

per_column.name: processing_lag_days
per_column.rationale: Quantifies delay between opening and processing, a process-quality facet an analyst can investigate for bottlenecks.

per_column.name: missing_source_id
per_column.rationale: Flags data-completeness/traceability gaps, a coherent facet of expense-record integrity and audit risk.

per_column.name: submitter_expense_count
per_column.rationale: Measures submitter activity/frequency, enabling detection of high-volume or anomalous submitters — relevant to spend oversight.

judge.rationale: The four columns collectively cohere around auditing/analyzing expense records for what is 'worth analyzing and actionable': spend magnitude (amount_tier), process timeliness (processing_lag_days), data integrity (missing_source_id), and submitter behavior (submitter_expense_count). These are genuine, data-inferable analytical facets rather than mechanical text metrics, so they meaningfully realise an inferred focus. The main weakness is that the facets span somewhat distinct sub-themes (spend risk vs. data quality vs. process latency vs. submitter profiling), so the single-focus centering is moderate rather than tight — an analyst could reasonably see this as a broad 'expense audit health' framing rather than one sharply defined focus. Granularity is useful and non-trivial (tiers, counts, lag, flag), and the implied focus (identifying actionable/risky expense patterns) is clearly actionable, hence the reasonably high but not top scores.
